# Path integral games with de Sitter $\alpha$ -vacua

**Authors:** Noah Miller Affiliation: School of Natural Sciences, Institute for Advanced Study, 1 Einstein Drive, Princeton, NJ 08540 USA Affiliation: Princeton Gravity Initiative, Princeton University, Jadwin Hall, Washington Road, Princeton NJ 08544, USA Email: noahmiller@ias.edu

## Abstract

The $\alpha$ -vacua are a 1-parameter family of quantum field vacua in de Sitter space which are invariant under the isometry group $SO(1,d)$ . In this work give a path integral construction of the de Sitter $\alpha$ -vacua. We explain that these states can be prepared by acting on the Bunch-Davies vacuum with a certain non-local charge operator. While most conserved charges live on a single codimension-1 manifold, we show that this particular charge lives on a pair of two codimension-1 manifolds which are antipodal mirrors of each other. The rules for the manipulation of this charge as an insertion in the path integral are explained. We further explain how this charge can be used to solve for the wavefunctionals of the $\alpha$ -vacua at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ (in the regime that $\alpha$ is small) by deforming the equator of de Sitter space to $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ / $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ .

We also discuss the special $\alpha$ -vacua known as the “in” and “out” vacua, for both heavy and light scalars. It is well known that the “in” and “out” vacua are equal in odd dimensions, but we also show that they are equal in even dimensions when $\sqrt{(d-1)^{2}/4-m^{2}}$ is a half-integer.

Finally, we investigate the question of whether the $\alpha$ -vacua can be constructed in interacting quantum field theories. Using the fact that the antipodal charge operator is only conserved in a free theory, we give a symmetry based argument that in general they cannot be, explaining why interactions and $SO(1,d)$ invariance of the vacua are in tension.

## 1 Introduction

A free quantum field theory of a scalar field in Minkowski space or Anti-de Sitter space has only a single vacuum state that is invariant under the full isometry group of the spacetime. The situation is different in de Sitter space, where there exists a 1-parameter family of states, called the $\alpha$ -vacua, which are invariant under the full de Sitter isometry group $SO(1,d)$ Chernikov and Tagirov (1968); Schomblond and Spindel (1976); Mottola (1985); Allen (1985); Burges (1984). The special case $\ket{\alpha= 0}$ is the Bunch-Davies vacuum Bunch and Davies (1978), also called the euclidean vacuum or the Hartle-Hawking vacuum Hartle and Hawking (1983).

These states have become a somewhat niche topic of recurring interest since their discovery in 1968 Chernikov and Tagirov (1968). Because the $\alpha$ -vacua are homogeneous and isotropic, many works have considered the possibility that the $\alpha$ -vacua (or states which look like the $\alpha$ -vacua above some short distance cut off) could have been initial conditions for the inflaton field in the early universe, and investigated what high energy physics would be imprinted in these states Kaloper et al. (2002); de Boer et al. (2005); Danielsson (2002a); Danielsson (2002b); Easther et al. (2001); Easther et al. (2003); Easther et al. (2002); Collins and Holman (2005). In quantum cosmology, Chen et al. (2024) found $\alpha$ -like states emerging in a system of two dS spacetimes connected by a euclidean wormhole. The $\alpha$ -vacua were also conjectured to be dual to marginal deformations of a dual CFT in the context of the dS/CFT correspondence Bousso et al. (2002); Ng and Strominger (2013); Spradlin and Volovich (2002). In the field of celestial holography, analog $\alpha$ -vacua have recently been defined in flat space which are not invariant under the full Poincaré group but are invariant under the Lorentz subgroup Melton et al. (2024). See Joung et al. (2006); Joung et al. (2007) for a group theory construction of the $\alpha$ -vacua. See also Kanno et al. (2014); Polyakov (2008); Nguyen (2017); Chopping et al. (2024); Ansari et al. (2024); Cotler and Strominger (2023).

The purpose of this note is, simply, to understand how the $\alpha$ -vacua are constructed using the Feynman path integral.

In 1984, it was noted by Burges11 1 who referenced an unpublished note by Gross and Witten Burges (1984) that there exists a certain non-local charge operator $\hat{Q}^{A}$ which generates the $\alpha$ -vacua from the Bunch-Davies vacuum via $\ket{\alpha}=e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\ket{0}$ . However, something was conspicuously missing from Burges’ paper which motivated this present investigation: it was not explained how the codimension-1 surface on which this charge was defined could be continuously deformed, in the way that surfaces can naturally be deformed when charges are conserved.

Let us be more precise. If we cover de Sitter space $dS_{d}=\mathbb{R}\times S_{d-1}$ with global coordinates $(t,\Omega)$ , with $\Omega\in S_{d-1}$ , as

$$ ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+\cosh^{2}(t)d\Omega_{d-1}^{2} $$

then Burges gave an expression for the charge that only holds on the $t=0$ slice:

$$ \hat{Q}^{A}=\int d^{d-1}\Omega\,\hat{\phi}(0,\Omega)\hat{\pi}(0,\Omega^{A}). $$

Here $\Omega^{A}$ is the point antipodal to $\Omega$ on the $S_{d-1}$ sphere. In this work we will explain how this charge can be defined beyond the $t=0$ slice. In fact, we will see that this charge actually lives on two antipodal slices in spacetime, and will study the consequences of this fact. This fact did not appear in Burges’ original analysis because the $t=0$ slice happens to be its own antipodal surface.

In section 2 we review global coordinates in de Sitter spacetime and in its euclidean analytic continuation.

In section 3 we review the path integral construction of the Bunch-Davies vacuum for a free scalar on a de Sitter background using the euclidean path integral on the half-sphere. We explain why this state is invariant under the dS isometry group.

In section 4 we discuss the well known fact that annihilation operators constructed out of “euclidean modes” (solutions to the dS Klein-Gordon equation which are non-singular when analytically continued to the lower half euclidean sphere) annihilate the Bunch-Davies state. We prove this fact with Noether’s theorem, which we are able to do because annihilation operators are the Noether charges of a linear symmetry that only exists in free theories.

In section 5 we discuss the antipodal map in de Sitter space, and use it to construct a non-local symmetry variation $\delta\phi=\epsilon\,\phi^{A}$ of the free scalar field. We calculate the associated classical conserved current using Noether’s theorem. This conserved current is unusual in that it is non-local, in the sense that the current evaluated a point in de Sitter space depends on the value of the field and its derivatives at that point and at the antipodal point. After quantization, we show that this classical conserved current is indeed promoted to a conserved insertion in the path integral à la a Ward–Takahashi identity, although the proof of this is slightly subtler than one might expect.

In section 6 we explain “why” extra dS isometry invariant states can be constructed aside from the Bunch-Davies vacuum. To briefly outline the argument, one would expect that a dS isometry invariant state could be constructed by acting on the Bunch-Davies state by some conserved charge, producing a state like $\hat{Q}\ket{0}$ for some $\hat{Q}$ which is defined as the integral over a codimension-1 surface of a locally-defined conserved current. However, the Bunch-Davies state is prepared by a path integral over the half-sphere, and the half-sphere is a simply-connected space, meaning the surface on which the conserved charge lives (the equator) is able to be contracted to zero, implying $\hat{Q}\ket{0}=0$ . However, due to the strange nature of the non-local “antipodal” charge $\hat{Q}^{A}$ , the equator together with its antipodal mirror are not able to be contracted on the lower half-sphere, so $\hat{Q}^{A}\ket{0}\neq 0$ and we can construct a family of dS-invariant states $\ket{\alpha}=e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\ket{0}$ .

In section 7 we explain which $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ result in $\ket{\alpha}$ being a normalizable state.

In section 8 we turn our attention to the so-called “in” and “out” vacuum states, which are special $\alpha$ -vacua that contain no particles in the infinite past/infinite future. Using a simple analytic argument, we are able to calculate which values of $\alpha$ produce these states. The argument uses the fact that the antipodal map in de Sitter space can be continuously connected to the identity via an analytic continuation through the euclidean section $t\mapsto t+i\pi$ . This argument works for all spacetime dimensions $d$ and mass $m$ . While it is well known that for heavy masses $m>\tfrac{d-1}{2}$ the in vacuum equals the out vacuum in odd dimensions Bousso et al. (2002); Lagogiannis et al. (2011), we show that for light masses $m<\tfrac{d-1}{2}$ the in vacuum also equals the out vacuum when $\sqrt{(d-1)^{2}/4-m^{2}}$ is a half-integer. This includes the massless and conformally coupled scalars.

In section 9 we discuss the $\alpha$ -vacua wavefunctionals at the infinite future of de Sitter space $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ . We use a path integral argument to find the operation which maps the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ to the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ when $\alpha$ is small. If $\alpha$ is finite, operator ordering problems prevent us from using our path integral argument to solve for the wavefunctional at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ , which we explain.

In section 10 we address the question of whether or not the $\alpha$ -vacua can be defined in interacting field theories. We argue that they cannot be. This is congruous with the findings of the previous works Collins et al. (2003); Danielsson (2002c); Einhorn and Larsen (2003a); Einhorn and Larsen (2003b); Goldstein and Lowe (2003); Goldstein and Lowe (2004); Goldstein (2005); Akhmedov (2014); Kaloper et al. (2002); Banks and Mannelli (2003); Akhmedov et al. (2023).

## 2 Global coordinates in lorentzian and euclidean de Sitter

Let us define a $d+1$ dimensional Minkowski embedding space with coordinates $X^{M}$ for $M=0,\ldots,d$ and metric $ds^{2}=-(dX^{0})^{2}+(dX^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(dX^{d})^{2}=\eta_{MN}dX^{M}dX^{N}$ . $d$ -dimensional de Sitter space $dS_{d}$ can be defined as a hyperboloid cut out of the embedding space

$$ -(X^{0})^{2}+(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1 $$

where we have set the de Sitter length scale to 1. Euclidean de Sitter space can then be defined via the analytic continuation

$$ X^{0}=-i\tilde{X}^{0} $$

where $\tilde{X}^{0}$ is taken to be real. Euclidean de Sitter space is a $d$ dimensional sphere $S_{d}$

$$ (\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1 $$

in an embedding space with metric $ds^{2}=(d\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+(dX^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(dX^{d})^{2}$ . Let us also define the lower half of the sphere $S_{d,-}\subset S_{d}$ to be

$$ S_{d,-}\equiv\{\tilde{X}^{0},\ldots,X^{d}\;|\;\tilde{X}^{0}\leq 0,(\tilde{X}^{0})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1\} $$

and the $X^{0}=\tilde{X}^{0}=0$ “equator” $E$ to be

$$ E\equiv\{X^{0},\ldots,X^{d}\;|\;X^{0}=0,(X^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=1\}. $$

The equator $E$ can be understood as a subset of either the lorentzian $dS_{d}$ or the euclidean $S_{d}$ .

*Figure 1: Lorentzian de Sitter space $dS_{d}$ and euclidean de Sitter space $S_{d}$ . The equator $E$ , defined at $X^{0}=\tilde{X}^{0}=0$ , exists on both. The halves of the euclidean sphere above and below $E$ are denoted $S_{d,+}$ and $S_{d,-}$ , respectively.*

Let $\Omega$ denote a set of sphere coordinates which cover the unit sphere $S_{d-1}$ with metric $d\Omega_{d-1}^{2}$ , and let $n^{a}(\Omega)$ with $a=1,\ldots,d$ be the unit vector on the sphere parameterized by $\Omega$ with $n(\Omega)^{2}=1$ . Then $dS_{d}$ may be parameterized with global coordinates $x^{\mu}=(t,\Omega)$ , for $\mu=0,\ldots,d-1$ , by

$$ \displaystyle X^{0}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=\sinh(t) \displaystyle X^{a}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=\cosh(t)n^{a}(\Omega) $$

with metric

$$ ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+\cosh^{2}(t)d\Omega^{2}_{d-1}. $$

If we analytically continue $t=-i\tilde{t}$ and take $\tilde{t}$ to be real, we make $X^{0}$ imaginary just as in (4). Euclidean de Sitter space $S_{d}$ is then parameterized as

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{X}^{0}(-i\tilde{t},\Omega) \displaystyle=\sin(\tilde{t}) \displaystyle X^{a}(-i\tilde{t},\Omega) \displaystyle=\cos(\tilde{t})n^{a}(\Omega) $$

where $\tilde{t}\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ . $\tilde{t}=-\pi/2$ is the south pole and $\tilde{t}=\pi/2$ is the north pole. The euclidean metric is

$$ ds^{2}=d\tilde{t}^{2}+\cos^{2}(\tilde{t})d\Omega^{2}_{d-1}. $$

We denote $\tilde{x}^{\mu}=(\tilde{t},\Omega)$ .

## 3 The Bunch-Davies state

In this section we review the path integral construction of the Bunch-Davies state in $dS_{d}$ . The euclidean action for a free scalar field $\phi$ of mass $m$ on a spacetime patch of the euclidean sphere $U\subset S_{d}$ is

$$ S_{U}[\phi]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{U}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\left((\nabla\phi)^{2}+m^{2}\phi^{2}\right). $$

The Bunch-Davies state, denoted as $\ket{0}$ , can be defined on the $\tilde{t}=0$ time slice $E$ as the euclidean path integral over the half-sphere with open boundary conditions. If $\varphi(\Omega)$ is some function on the equatorial $d-1$ sphere, then let us define the field “position eigenvector” state $\ket{\varphi}$ to be the state that satisfies

$$ \hat{\phi}(0,\Omega)\ket{\varphi}=\varphi(\Omega)\ket{\varphi}. $$

The Bunch-Davies wavefunctional evaluated at $\varphi$ is then given by the path integral over all fields $\phi$ on the half-sphere which are equal to $\varphi$ on $E$ . See figure 2.

$$ \Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]=\innerproduct{\varphi}{0}=\int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}. $$

*Figure 2: Definition of the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional $\Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]$ as a euclidean path integral on the half-sphere with boundary conditions $\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\varphi$ .*

The group of isometries of $dS_{d}$ is $SO(1,d)$ . Let us define the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(1,d)$ vector fields as

$$ L^{MN}\equiv\eta^{NP}X^{M}\partialderivative{X^P}-\eta^{MP}X^{N}\partialderivative{X^P} $$

and denote $\hat{L}^{MN}$ to be the corresponding quantum operators. Generators of the form $L^{0M}$ are “boost” vector fields, while generators of the form $L^{MN}$ with $M,N=1,\ldots,d$ are “spatial rotation” vector fields which generate a $SO(d)\subset SO(1,d)$ subgroup. Only the spatial rotations map $E$ into itself.

One might wonder if $\ket{0}$ is invariant under all of these symmetries. Clearly, $\ket{0}$ is invariant under the $SO(d)$ subgroup because the euclidean half-sphere itself is symmetric under these rotations. But what about the boost generators $\hat{L}^{0M}$ ? Do they annihilate $\ket{0}$ ? Without loss of generality we focus on $\hat{L}^{01}$ .

*Figure 3: The Killing vector field $L^{01}$ generates a boost in lorentzian de Sitter and a rotation in euclidean de Sitter.*

Notice that in the euclidean section, the vector field is

$$ -iL^{01}=-\tilde{X}^{0}\partialderivative{X^1}+X^{1}\partialderivative{\tilde{X}^0} $$

and generates a $U(1)$ rotation in the $\tilde{X}^{0}$ - $X^{1}$ plane. See figure 3. This means that, if $\epsilon$ is a tiny angle, then in euclidean de Sitter space the operator $1-\epsilon\,\hat{L}^{01}$ has the effect of rotating the path integral by an angle of $\epsilon$ in said plane. (For a review on how the quantum operators corresponding to spacetime vector fields shift the spacetime boundary of path integration, see appendix A.)

However, due to the $SO(d+1)$ symmetry of $S_{d}$ , we can trivially see that the rotated path integral equals the original path integral, and thus $\hat{L}^{01}\ket{0}=0$ . See figure 4. If our path integral had, say, contained insertions on the lower half-sphere, then the state would not have been annihilated by $\hat{L}^{01}$ . See figure 5.

*Figure 4: Proof of the de Sitter invariance of the Bunch-Davies state. $\epsilon\hat{L}^{01}$ rotates the euclidean half-sphere by angle $\epsilon$ , which does not actually change the path integral.*

*Figure 5: If we were to add some insertions into the half-sphere path integral, the corresponding state would not be annihilated by $\hat{L}^{01}$ because the rotation of the equator by a tiny angle $\epsilon$ would not leave the path integral invariant.*

We have now seen that the Bunch-Davies state is invariant under the full dS isometry group. This is a special property, and one may wonder if there are more states invariant under this group. As we will see, the $\alpha$ -vacua are a 1-parmeter family of states which are also dS-invariant.

## 4 Noether’s theorem and annihilation operators

In this section we review some properties of annihilation operators, euclidean modes, and their relation to the Bunch-Davies state.

Consider a function $f$ on $dS_{d}$ which satisfies the free de Sitter Klein-Gordon equation of motion

$$ (\nabla^{2}-m^{2})f=0. $$

$f$ can also be understood as a function on the sphere $S_{d}$ upon analytic continuation.

On the euclidean sphere $S_{d}$ , the eigenvalues of the Laplace operator $\nabla^{2}$ are given by $-l(l+d-1)$ for all $l=0,1,2\ldots$ . Notice, then, that $\nabla^{2}$ only has negative eigenvalues while any $f$ which solves (17) will be an eigenfunction of $\nabla^{2}$ with the positive eigenvalue $m^{2}$ . This implies that, strictly speaking, there exists no such $f$ which is defined on the whole sphere. Any $f$ that solves (17) must be ill-defined at some points on $S_{d}$ , where there will be non-analyticities such as poles or branch cuts.

If the analytic continuation of a function $f_{e}$ that solves (17) is well-defined on the whole lower half-sphere $S_{d,-}$ , we call it a “euclidean mode.” As a consequence of the previous discussion, all euclidean modes must necessarily have non-analyticities or singularities in the upper half-sphere $S_{d,+}$ .

Every solution $f$ to the Klein-Gordon equation can be used to define an associated “annihilation operator” $\hat{a}(f)$ . It turns out that any annihilation operator built out of a euclidean mode will annihilate the Bunch-Davies state, $\hat{a}(f_{e})\ket{0}=0$ . We will now present a proof of this fact using Noether’s theorem.

Classically, the free euclidean action of a scalar field $S_{U}[\phi]$ possesses a symmetry

$$ \delta\phi=\epsilon f $$

where $\epsilon$ is a tiny constant and $f$ is any function which satisfies (17). This symmetry only exists because the free equation of motion is linear, and any two solutions can be added together to produce a new solution.

We will now preform the Noether trick to find the conserved current corresponding to this symmetry. To do this, we promote $\epsilon$ to an infinitesimal function $\varepsilon(\tilde{x})$ which vanishes at the boundary of $U$ , and consider the change in the action corresponding to $\delta\phi(\tilde{x})=\varepsilon(\tilde{x})f(\tilde{x})$ . It turns out to be

$$ \delta S_{U}[\phi]=\int_{U}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\left((\partial^{\mu}\varepsilon)(f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\phi)-(\varepsilon\,\phi)(\nabla^{2}f-m^{2}f)\right) $$

where $f_{1}\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}f_{2}\equiv f_{1}(\partial_{\mu}f_{2})-(\partial_{\mu}f_{1})f_{2}$ . Because $f$ satisfies (17) and $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, this implies that the Noether current

$$ J(f)_{\mu}\equiv f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\phi $$

is conserved on shell, satisfying $\nabla_{\mu}J(f)^{\mu}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{g}}\partial_{\mu}(\sqrt{g}J(f)^{\mu})=0$ . Let us define the associated conserved charge

$$ a_{\Sigma}(f)\equiv i\int_{\Sigma}d\Sigma^{\mu}J(f)_{\mu}. $$

which is defined on a codimension- $1$ surface $\Sigma$ . This conserved charge is the classical version of the annihilation operator corresponding to the mode $f$ . (We note that the standard definition of the annihilation operator differs from the one above by an extra complex conjugation, replacing $f$ above with $f^{*}$ .)

We now turn to the quantum path integral on the lower half euclidean sphere. If we define $\phi^{\prime}=\phi+\varepsilon f_{e}$ , then $\mathcal{D}\phi^{\prime}=\mathcal{D}\phi$ because the addition of $\varepsilon f_{e}$ simply shifts the measure. Crucially, because $f_{e}$ is a euclidean mode, the change in measure $\phi^{\prime}=\phi+\varepsilon f_{e}$ is well defined everywhere on the lower half-sphere.

Using this symmetry variation, one can derive a corresponding quantum Ward identity in the usual way, and it will read

$$ \int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}\nabla_{\mu}J(f_{e})^{\mu}(\tilde{x})=0 $$

where $\tilde{x}$ can be any point in $S_{d,-}$ .

The above equation implies that, if one inserts the charge $a_{\Sigma}(f_{e})$ into the path integral, $\Sigma$ can be deformed without changing the path integral.

Let us now define the quantum annihilation operator22 2 In this paper we use hatted symbols to denote operators acting on states, such as $\hat{a}(f)$ , and non-hatted symbols to denote insertions in the path integral, like $a_{\Sigma}(f)$ .

$$ \hat{a}(f)\equiv i\int_{E}dE^{\mu}f\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\hat{\phi} $$

where we set the codimension-1 surface $\Sigma$ to be the equator $E$ .

*Figure 6: If $f_{e}$ has no singularities on $S_{d,-}$ , then $\hat{a}(f_{e})$ annihilates $\ket{0}$ because the equator is contractible.*

Because $E$ is contractable on the half-sphere, the annihilation operator $\hat{a}(f_{e})$ annihilates the Bunch-Davies state, as shown in figure 6.

$$ (\hat{a}(f_{e})\Psi_{0}^{E})[\varphi]=\int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}a_{E}(f_{e})=0. $$

This completes the proof.

## 5 The antipodal symmetry, classically and quantumly

One can define an antipodal map on de Sitter space, which takes the form $X\mapsto-X$ in the embedding space. This map commutes with the dS isometry group $SO(1,d)$ .

Interestingly, one cannot define an analogous antipodal map in Anti-de Sitter space. This is essentially because Anti-de Sitter space is defined as the universal cover of the hyperboloid $-(X^{0})^{2}-(X^{1})^{2}+(X^{2})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=-1$ in flat space with signature $(2,d-1)$ , which has closed timelike curves and must be “unwrapped.” Once unwrapped, however, the point $-X$ has an infinite number of representatives in the covering space, and as a result there is no way to continuously lift the antipodal map.33 3 Furthermore, a $SO(1,d-1)$ invariant antipodal map cannot be defined in euclidean Anti-de Sitter space (EAdS) either. EAdS can be defined as the “top cap” of the hyperboloid $-(X^{0})^{2}+(\tilde{X}^{1})^{2}+\ldots+(X^{d})^{2}=-1$ . The natural embedding space antipodal map $X\mapsto-X$ maps the “top cap” with $X^{0}>0$ into the “bottom cap” with $X^{0}<0$ , and thus does not map EAdS into itself. If one tries to adopt an ad-hoc discontinuous definition of the antipodal map on the universal cover, said map will not be $SO(2,d-1)$ invariant. See figure 7.

If one attempts to define $-X$ as the antipode of $X$ in the embedding space hyperboloid, there will not be a well defined meaning to $-X$ in the universal cover of the hyperboloid, as it could be one of an infinite number of possibilities.*

Going back to de Sitter, where points are parameterized by $x=(t,\Omega)\in dS_{d}$ with $\Omega\in S_{d-1}$ , let us define $\Omega^{A}$ to be the point on the unit $S_{d-1}$ sphere antipodal to $\Omega$ . For each $x$ let us define the antipodal point $x^{A}$ to be

$$ x^{A}\equiv(-t,\Omega^{A}). $$

For a point in euclidean de Sitter space $\tilde{x}=(\tilde{t},\Omega)\in S_{d}$ , we similarly define

$$ \tilde{x}^{A}\equiv(-\tilde{t},\Omega^{A}). $$

For a function $\phi$ on de Sitter space (either lorentzian or euclidean) denote $\phi^{A}$ to be the antipodally-flipped function

$$ \phi^{A}(t,\Omega)\equiv\phi(-t,\Omega^{A}),\hskip 28.45274pt\phi^{A}(-i\tilde{t},\Omega)=\phi(i\tilde{t},\Omega^{A}). $$

If $\phi$ solves the equation of motion $(\nabla^{2}-m^{2})\phi=0$ , then $\phi^{A}$ will solve it as well. This enables us to define a certain symmetry transformation which will play a prominent role in the rest of this paper. Due to the linearity of the equation of motion for the free scalar field, we may consider the symmetry transformation

$$ \delta\phi=\epsilon\,\phi^{A} $$

where $\epsilon$ is a tiny constant. This infinitesimal variation exponentiates to the finite transformation

$$ \phi^{\prime}=\cosh(\alpha)\phi+\sinh(\alpha)\phi^{A} $$

for finite parameter $\alpha$ .

The variation (28) is similar to a variation we previously considered, (18), except that now the linear shift in the field $\phi$ is field-dependent.

Let us now use the Noether trick to find the corresponding conserved current. We promote $\epsilon$ to a tiny function $\varepsilon(\tilde{x})$ . The variation of the euclidean action on the spacetime patch $U\subset S_{d}$ under variation $\delta\phi(\tilde{x})=\varepsilon(\tilde{x})\phi^{A}(\tilde{x})$ is

$$ \delta S_{U}[\phi]=\int_{U}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\left((\partial^{\mu}\varepsilon)J^{A}_{\mu}-(\varepsilon\,\phi)(\nabla^{2}\phi^{A}-m^{2}\phi^{A})\right) $$

where we required that $\varepsilon$ vanishes on $\partial U$ and have defined the current

$$ J^{A}_{\mu}\equiv\phi^{A}\overset{\leftrightarrow}{\partial}_{\mu}\phi. $$

Because the antipodal map $X\mapsto-X$ commutes with the dS isometry group, the current $J^{A}_{\mu}$ transforms like a proper spin-1 current under said isometry group.

Using (30), because $\varepsilon$ is an arbitrary function we know that

$$ \nabla^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}=-\phi(\nabla^{2}-m^{2})\phi^{A}=0 $$

is satisfied on-shell and thus $\nabla^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}=0$ because $\phi^{A}$ solves the equation of motion.

Notice that $J^{A}_{\mu}$ is not a locally-defined current. $J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})$ depends on the values of $\phi$ at both $\tilde{x}$ and $\tilde{x}^{A}$ . In fact, in (30), while we are ostensibly integrating over points in the subset $U\subset S_{d}$ , the expression also depends on the value of $\phi$ at points outside of $U$ , in the antipodally-flipped version of $U$ we could call $U^{A}$ .

We’re interested in investigating how the classical conservation law (32) manifests as a path integral Ward identity after quantization. Let us first review how standard Ward identities are derived before showing how the Ward identity for $J^{A}_{\mu}$ deviates from the usual story. Say that we have some local symmetry variation $\phi\mapsto\phi+\epsilon\,\delta_{\rm var}\phi$ of our euclidean action (12) where $\epsilon$ is a tiny constant. Promoting $\epsilon$ to a function $\varepsilon(\tilde{x})$ and considering the variation $\delta\phi=\varepsilon\,\delta_{\rm var}\phi$ , the action will vary as

$$ \delta S_{S_{d}}[\phi]=\int_{S_{d}}d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\,\varepsilon\nabla^{\mu}J_{\mu} $$

where $J_{\mu}$ is the Noether current of $\delta_{\rm var}\phi$ . Then, defining $\phi^{\prime}=\phi+\varepsilon\delta_{\rm var}\phi$ and assuming $\mathcal{D}\phi^{\prime}=\mathcal{D}\phi$ (meaning there is no anomaly) we have

$$ \displaystyle\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]} \displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}\phi^{\prime}e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi^{\prime}]} \displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}\phi(1-\int d^{d}\tilde{x}\sqrt{g}\,\varepsilon\,\nabla^{\mu}J_{\mu})e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]} $$

and thus

$$ \int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\nabla^{\mu}J_{\mu}(\tilde{x})=0 $$

for any $\tilde{x}\in S_{d}$ . This is a traditional Ward identity.

For our antipodal symmetry variation (28), the story is complicated somewhat. That’s because the variation of the action (30) does not look like the usual (33), due to the $\phi(\nabla^{2}-m^{2})\phi^{A}$ term. Of course, classically, this term vanishes on shell, but in the quantum path integral we are integrating over off-shell fields so it is not a priori clear if it vanishes.

If we attempt to repeat the standard Ward identity derivation using the antipodal variation (28), from (30) we see that we’ll get44 4 The antipodal variation has no anomaly because $\det( \begin{smallmatrix} \cosh(\alpha) & \sinh(\alpha) \\ \sinh(\alpha) & \cosh(\alpha) \end{smallmatrix} )=1$ .

$$ \int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\nabla^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})=-\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}(\phi(\nabla^{2}-m^{2})\phi^{A})(\tilde{x}). $$

Note that the RHS is not obviously zero. However, because we know that the two point function

$$ \langle\phi(\tilde{x})\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime})\rangle=\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\phi(\tilde{x})\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime}) $$

satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\sqrt{g(\tilde{x})}(\nabla_{\tilde{x}}^{2}-m^{2})\langle\phi(\tilde{x})\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime})\rangle \displaystyle=-\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\frac{\delta S_{S_{d}}}{\delta\phi(\tilde{x})}\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,\frac{\delta}{\delta\phi(\tilde{x})}\left(e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\right)\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime}) \displaystyle=-\int\mathcal{D}\phi\,\left(e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\right)\frac{\delta\phi(\tilde{x}^{\prime})}{\delta\phi(\tilde{x})} \displaystyle=-\delta^{(4)}(\tilde{x}-\tilde{x}^{\prime}), $$

we know that, because $\tilde{x}$ and $\tilde{x}^{A}$ are never coincident, we have

$$ (\nabla_{\tilde{x}}^{2}-m^{2})\langle\phi(\tilde{x})\phi(\tilde{x}^{A})\rangle=0. $$

Thus the RHS of (36) is indeed 0 for all $\tilde{x}$ . This implies that $\nabla^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}=0$ really does hold as a quantum Ward identity, satisfying

$$ \int\mathcal{D}\phi\,e^{-S_{S_{d}}[\phi]}\nabla^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})=0. $$

We can now construct a charge $Q_{\Sigma}^{A}$ by integrating $J^{A}_{\mu}$ over a codimension-1 surface $\Sigma$ (and multiplying by $1/2$ ).

$$ Q_{\Sigma}^{A}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Sigma}d\Sigma^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}. $$

We refer to this as the “antipodal charge.” This charge first appeared in the work of Burges Burges (1984), who considered it only on the equitorial sliced $\Sigma=E$ . The advantage of our current discussion is that we are able to see that, because $J^{A}_{\mu}$ is conserved, we can freely deform $\Sigma$ and $Q_{\Sigma}^{A}$ will not change. However, it is important to note that because $J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})$ depends on the field at both $\tilde{x}$ and $\tilde{x}^{A}$ , we know that $Q_{\Sigma}^{A}$ depends on field values at both $\Sigma$ and on the antipodally-flipped version of $\Sigma$ , which we can call $\Sigma^{A}$ . See figure 8. For certain surfaces, $\Sigma$ and $\Sigma^{A}$ are actually the same surface, such as when $\Sigma$ is the equator $E$ .

## 6 Why the dS-invariant $\alpha$ -vacua can be constructed

In section 3, we defined the Bunch-Davies state $\ket{0}$ and showed it was dS-invariant (i.e., invariant under the group of dS isometries). We now ask, how can we construct further dS-invariant states?

One possible method of constructing another dS-invariant state would be to act on $\ket{0}$ with some conserved charge, $\hat{Q}$ . Here we are imagining that $\hat{Q}$ is defined as an integral over the equator $E$ of some locally-defined conserved current $J_{\mu}$ , where $J_{\mu}$ itself transforms like a proper vector field under the dS isometry group.

Let us review why $\hat{Q}\ket{0}$ must be dS-invariant. Clearly it is invariant under the $SO(d)$ subgroup of spatial rotations, meaning the non-trivial step is to check that $\hat{L}^{01}\hat{Q}\ket{0}=0$ . We’ll accomplish this by proving $[\hat{L}^{01},\hat{Q}]=0$ .

First, we insert $Q_{E}$ on the equator in the sphere path integral. (We can also put some extra arbitrary insertions into the upper or lower half-sphere in the path integral in order to prepare arbitrary bra and ket states.) Then we surround the equator by two dS-isometry generator operator insertions defined just above and below the equator, which are $1-\epsilon L^{01}_{E_{\rm above}}$ and $1+\epsilon L^{01}_{E_{\rm below}}$ respectively, where $\epsilon$ is a tiny angle. Because the current $J_{\mu}$ which $Q$ is an integral of transforms like a spin-1 vector, $1-\epsilon L^{01}_{E_{\rm above}}$ and $1+\epsilon L^{01}_{E_{\rm below}}$ will have the effect of rotating the surface on which $Q$ is defined by the angle $\epsilon$ . We denote this new rotated surface as $E^{\prime}$ . See figure 9. Because $Q$ is conserved, however, we are able to rotate $E^{\prime}$ back to $E$ . This implies $[\hat{L}^{01},\hat{Q}]=0$ as an operator equation (as the extra insertions in the upper and lower half-sphere are completely arbitrary), which is what we wanted to show.

*Figure 9: The argument that conserved charges commute with the de Sitter isometry generators. Arbitrary insertions are drawn in the upper and lower half-sphere to allow arbitrary bra and ket states to be prepared.*

*Figure 10: Locally-defined conserved charges will annihilate the Bunch-Davies state because the equator $E$ can be contracted.*

We have now shown that $\hat{Q}\ket{0}$ is dS-invariant. However, there is a problem. Because $E$ is contractible on the half-sphere, the charge $\hat{Q}$ will actually annihilate the Bunch-Davies vacuum and $\hat{Q}\ket{0}=0$ ! See figure 10. So, while $\hat{Q}\ket{0}$ is dS-invariant for any locally-defined $\hat{Q}$ , it is also zero.

However, our antipodal charge $Q^{A}$ has a unique property that locally-defined charges do not have: it is not contractible in the usual way, and this implies that $\hat{Q}^{A}\ket{0}\neq 0$ .

To see why this is the case, consider the path integral expression for $\hat{Q}^{A}\ket{0}$ :

$$ (\hat{Q}^{A}\Psi_{0})[\varphi]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\evaluated{\phi}_{E}=\,\varphi}\mathcal{D}\phi\;e^{-S_{S_{d,-}}[\phi]}\int_{E}dE^{\mu}J^{A}_{\mu}. $$

Because the equator $E$ is contractible on the half-sphere and $J^{A}_{\mu}$ is conserved, we might still expect that we could contract $E$ and the state would be zero. However, recall that $J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})$ depends on both $\phi(\tilde{x})$ and $\phi(\tilde{x}^{A})$ , and the path integral above only integrates over values of $\phi(\tilde{x})$ for $\tilde{x}$ contained in the lower half-sphere. This implies that we are disallowed from inserting $J^{A}_{\mu}(\tilde{x})$ anywhere on the lower half-sphere, aside from the equator itself.

Because the antipodal mirror of $E$ would venture into the upper half-sphere as we contract $E$ in the lower half-sphere, we are therefore not allowed to contract the equator after acting $Q_{E}^{A}$ on the half-sphere, and this is why $\hat{Q}^{A}\ket{0}\neq 0$ . See figure 11. This is the fact that lets us construct an infinite number of dS-invariant states.

Explicitly, the charge $\hat{Q}^{A}$ on the $t=0$ slice is equal to

$$ \hat{Q}^{A}=\int d^{d-1}\Omega\;\hat{\phi}(0,\Omega)\hat{\pi}(0,\Omega^{A}) $$

where $d^{d-1}\Omega$ is the measure on the unit $S_{d-1}$ . The commutator of this charge with the field operator and momentum operator is55 5 Note that we defined the charge $Q^{A}$ with an extra factor of $1/2$ in (41). And yet, in (44) we see that $\hat{Q}^{A}$ does generate the original antipodal symmetry (28) from which our Noether charge was constructed. It is strange that the charge requires an ad hoc multiplication by $1/2$ in order to generate the correct symmetry. This runs counter to the usual state of affairs, where the Noether charge generates the original symmetry under the commutator exactly.

$$ [\hat{\phi}(0,\Omega),\hat{Q}^{A}]=i\hat{\phi}(0,\Omega^{A}),\hskip 28.45274pt[\hat{\pi}(0,\Omega),\hat{Q}^{A}]=-i\hat{\pi}(0,\Omega^{A}). $$

We can exponentiate this charge to get a 1-parameter family of dS-invariant states

$$ \ket{\alpha}\equiv e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\ket{0}. $$

These are the $\alpha$ -vacua. They are not annihilated by the euclidean modes, but rather by a Bogoliubov transformation of the euclidean modes. From the relation

$$ e^{i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}\hat{a}(f)e^{-i\alpha\hat{Q}^{A}}=\cosh(\alpha)\hat{a}(f)-\sinh(\alpha)\hat{a}(f^{A}) $$

we know that the $\alpha$ -vacua satisfy

$$ \Big(\cosh(\alpha)\hat{a}(f_{e})-\sinh(\alpha)\hat{a}(f_{e}^{A})\Big)\ket{\alpha}=0 $$

where $f_{e}$ is any euclidean mode.

*Figure 11: In the half-sphere path integral, the antipodal charge integrated over the equator cannot be contracted to zero, because the points on the lower half-sphere have their antipodes in the upper half-sphere, and the field values there are not being integrated over in the path integral.*

## 7 Normalizability of $\alpha$ -vacua wavefunctionals

In principle, $\alpha$ can be a complex number if one does not mind having a non CPT-invariant vacuum. However, $\ket{\alpha}$ won’t be normalizable for all $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ . In this section we solve for the allowed range of $\alpha$ for which $\ket{\alpha}$ is normalizable, replicating the findings of Chernikov and Tagirov (1968); Burges (1984).

The wavefunctionals of the $\alpha$ -vacua $\Psi^{E}_{\alpha}[\varphi]=\innerproduct{\varphi}{\alpha}$ on the equator are related to the wavefunctional of the Bunch-Davies state $\Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]$ via

$$ \Psi^{E}_{\alpha}[\varphi]=\Psi^{E}_{0}\left[\cosh(\alpha)\varphi+\sinh(\alpha)\varphi^{A}\right]. $$

Because $\Psi^{E}_{0}$ has short distance singularities, i.e., a diverging amount of correlation between nearby field variables, the above equation tells us that $\Psi^{E}_{\alpha}$ has both short-distance and “antipodal-short-distance” singularities, where there is a high-degree of correlation between field values at antipodal points.

First, we define a basis of spherical harmonics on the $d-1$ sphere $Y_{\ell m}(\Omega)$ , where $\ell=0,1,2,\ldots$ and $m$ is a generalized multi-index. Let us assume all the spherical harmonics are real

$$ Y_{\ell m}(\Omega)^{*}=Y_{\ell m}(\Omega) $$

and normalized such that

$$ \int d^{d-1}\Omega\,Y_{\ell m}(\Omega)Y_{\ell^{\prime}m^{\prime}}(\Omega)=\delta_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\delta_{mm^{\prime}}. $$

Under the antipodal map, the spherical harmonics satisfy

$$ Y_{\ell m}(\Omega^{A})=(-1)^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega). $$

Let us expand the test function $\varphi$ on the equatorial $d-1$ sphere into a basis of spherical harmonics as

$$ \varphi(\Omega)=\sum_{\ell,m}c_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega). $$

The norm of $\ket{\alpha}$ on the $t=0$ time slice is given by

$$ \innerproduct{\alpha}{\alpha}=\int\prod_{\ell,m}dc_{\ell m}\Psi^{E*}_{\alpha}[\varphi]\Psi^{E}_{\alpha}[\varphi]. $$

The Bunch-Davies state on the equator $E$ is a gaussian wavefunctional

$$ \Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{E}_{0}\exp(-\sum_{\ell,m} B^{E}_{0,\ell} (c_{\ell m})^2) $$

where $\mathcal{N}^{E}_{0}$ is a normalization constant and $B^{E}_{0,\ell}$ are a collection of positive real coefficients. We won’t need the exact expressions for $B^{E}_{0,\ell}$ , but they can be found in Burges (1984) for dimensions $d=2,3,4$ .

Let us now write down the wavefunctional for the $\alpha$ -vacuum. Using (51), we have the equation

$$ \cosh(\alpha)Y_{\ell m}(\Omega)+\sinh(\alpha)Y_{\ell m}(\Omega^{A})=e^{(-1)^{\ell}\alpha}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega) $$

and by (48), we then have

$$ \Psi^{E}_{\alpha}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{E}_{0}\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} e^{(-1)^\ell 2 \alpha} B^{E}_{0,\ell} (c_{\ell m})^2 ). $$

The $\alpha$ -vacuum is therefore normalizable if and only if $\real(e^{2\alpha})>0$ and $\real(e^{-2\alpha})>0$ , which is equivalent to just

$$ \real(e^{2\alpha})>0. $$

As a final observation, from the expression of the wavefunctional (56), we can also see that the $\alpha$ which parameterize $\ket{\alpha}$ are periodic up to shifts in $\pi i$ .

$$ \ket{\alpha+ \pi i}=\ket{\alpha}. $$

## 8 In and Out vacua

### 8.1 Definition of in/out states

The “in” and “out” vacua in de Sitter space are dS-invariant vacuum states in which the quantum fields obey definite exponential fall-offs at $t=\pm\infty$ . It turns out that these “in” and “out” vacua are actually $\alpha$ -vacua for special values of $\alpha$ . In this section we review the definition the in/out vacua and compute these values of $\alpha$ using a simple argument.

The classical equation of motion for a free scalar field in de Sitter space is

$$ (\nabla^{2}-m^{2})\phi=\Big(-\partial_{t}^{2}-(d-1)\tanh t\,\partial_{t}+\frac{\nabla^{2}_{S_{d-1}}}{\cosh^{2}t}-m^{2}\Big)\phi=0. $$

At $t\to\pm\infty$ , solutions to this equation have the form

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\phi(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=A(\Omega)e^{-h_{+}t}+B(\Omega)e^{-h_{-}t}+\ldots, \displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}\phi(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=C(\Omega)e^{+h_{+}t}+D(\Omega)e^{+h_{-}t}+\ldots, $$

where $A(\Omega)$ , $B(\Omega)$ , $C(\Omega)$ , $D(\Omega)$ are arbitrary sphere functions, the “ $\ldots$ ” terms are terms of order $\mathcal{O}(e^{-(h_{+}+2)|t|})$ and $\mathcal{O}(e^{-(h_{-}+2)|t|})$ , and $h_{+}$ and $h_{-}$ satisfy

$$ h_{\pm}^{2}-(d-1)h_{\pm}+m^{2}=0 $$

and are given by

$$ h_{\pm}=\frac{d-1}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right)^{2}-m^{2}}. $$

These solutions behave qualitatively differently depending on if $m$ is bigger or smaller than $(d-1)/2$ . For a “heavy scalar” with $m>(d-1)/2$ , $h_{+}$ and $h_{-}$ are complex numbers and conjugates of each other. For a “light scalar” with $0<m<(d-1)/2$ , $h_{\pm}$ are two positive real numbers.

Say you have some solutions to the wave equation (59) called $f^{\rm out}_{+}$ , $f^{\rm out}_{-}$ , $f^{\rm in}_{+}$ , $f^{\rm in}_{-}$ , which at $t=\pm\infty$ satisfy

$$ \displaystyle f^{\rm out}_{+}(t,\Omega)=A(\Omega)e^{-h_{+}t}\hskip 14.22636pt \displaystyle f^{\rm out}_{-}(t,\Omega)=B(\Omega)e^{-h_{-}t} \displaystyle\text{ as }t\to\infty \displaystyle f^{\rm in}_{+}(t,\Omega)=C(\Omega)e^{+h_{+}t}\hskip 14.22636pt \displaystyle f^{\rm in}_{-}(t,\Omega)=D(\Omega)e^{+h_{-}t} \displaystyle\text{ as }t\to-\infty $$

for some arbitrary functions $A$ , $B$ , $C$ , $D$ . The in/out vacua are the states which satisfy

$$ \displaystyle\hat{a}(f^{\rm out}_{-})\ket{{\rm out},+}=0, \displaystyle\hat{a}(f^{\rm in}_{-})\ket{{\rm in},+}=0, \displaystyle\hat{a}(f^{\rm out}_{+})\ket{{\rm out},-}=0, \displaystyle\hat{a}(f^{\rm in}_{+})\ket{{\rm in},-}=0, $$

for all possible $f^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}$ . We alert the reader that not all of these states will be normalizable, as we’ll soon see.

### 8.2 Calculating $\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}$ using a simple argument

Consider a function $f_{e}(t,\Omega)$ which is a euclidean mode solution to (59), meaning it is non-singular when analytically continued to the lower half euclidean sphere. On the upper half-sphere it may have poles and branch cuts, as depicted in figure 12.

At $t=\pm\infty$ , $f_{e}(t,\Omega)$ must behave as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}f_{e}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=A(\Omega)e^{-h_{+}t}+B(\Omega)e^{-h_{-}t}+\ldots, \displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}f_{e}(t,\Omega) \displaystyle=C(\Omega)e^{+h_{+}t}+D(\Omega)e^{+h_{-}t}+\ldots, $$

for some functions $A,B,C,D$ , just like any solution to (59) must.

Let us now consider the behavior of the function $f_{e}(t+\pi i,\Omega)$ (which also solves (59)) at $t=\pm\infty$ . It behaves as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}f_{e}(t+\pi i,\Omega) \displaystyle=e^{-\pi ih_{+}}A(\Omega)e^{-h_{+}t}+e^{-\pi ih_{-}}B(\Omega)e^{-h_{-}t}+\ldots, \displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}f_{e}(t+\pi i,\Omega) \displaystyle=e^{+\pi ih_{+}}C(\Omega)e^{+h_{+}t}+e^{+\pi ih_{+}}D(\Omega)e^{+h_{-}t}+\ldots. $$

In the embedding space parameterization of de Sitter $X^{M}(t,\Omega)$ (8), note that

$$ X^{M}(t+\pi i,\Omega)=-X^{M}(t,\Omega) $$

so $t\mapsto t+\pi i$ acts the same as the antipodal map.

*Figure 12: The analytic structure of a euclidean mode $f_{e}$ on the euclidean sphere.*

At a first glance, it seems as though $t\mapsto t-\pi i$ would also correspond to the antipodal map, however there is a key difference between $t+\pi i$ and $t-\pi i$ . Recalling our notation $t=-i\tilde{t}$ , consider the how the surface $\tilde{t}=w$ evolves on the sphere as $w$ is smoothly interpolated from $0$ to $-\pi$ . The surface $\tilde{t}=0$ is the $S_{d-1}$ equator, and then as $w$ decreases, the $S_{d-1}$ moves downward on the euclidean $S_{d}$ sphere, shrinks to a point at the south pole when $w=-\pi/2$ , and then moves back up the sphere until it reaches the equator again at $\tilde{t}=-\pi$ , but flipped antipodally. This is shown in figure 13. Therefore, $f_{e}(\pi i,\Omega)=f_{e}(0,\Omega^{A})$ . Likewise, one can show that a point just above the equator $(\epsilon,\Omega)$ gets mapped to an antipodal point just under the equator $(-\epsilon,\Omega^{A})$ under $\tilde{t}\mapsto\tilde{t}-\pi$ , implying $(\partial_{t}f_{e})(\pi i,\Omega)=-(\partial_{t}f_{e})(0,\Omega^{A})$ . Because $f_{e}(t+\pi i,\Omega)$ is guaranteed to also solve the second order wave equation (59), these properties imply that all euclidean modes $f_{e}$ satisfy

$$ f_{e}(t+\pi i,\Omega)=f_{e}^{A}(t,\Omega)=f_{e}(-t,\Omega^{A}) $$

for all $t,\Omega$ . The same could not necessarily be said for $f_{e}(t-\pi i,\Omega)$ , because any path that travels through the upper half-sphere may encounter poles or branch cuts which cannot be safely navigated through.

*Figure 13: As the surface $\tilde{t}=0$ is smoothly interpolated to $\tilde{t}=-\pi$ , the surface passes through the south pole and comes out antipodally flipped.*

If we use (65), (66), and (68), we can engineer in/out modes with the falloffs $h_{\pm}$ at $t=\pm\infty$ via the linear combinations

$$ \displaystyle f_{e}(x)-e^{+\pi ih_{+}}f_{e}(x^{A})\sim e^{-h_{-}t}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{at }t\to+\infty \displaystyle f_{e}(x)-e^{+\pi ih_{-}}f_{e}(x^{A})\sim e^{-h_{+}t}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{at }t\to+\infty \displaystyle f_{e}(x)-e^{-\pi ih_{+}}f_{e}(x^{A})\sim e^{+h_{-}t}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{at }t\to-\infty \displaystyle f_{e}(x)-e^{-\pi ih_{-}}f_{e}(x^{A})\sim e^{+h_{+}t}\hskip 28.45274pt\text{at }t\to-\infty $$

where we remind the reader that $f_{e}$ could be any euclidean mode. Comparing the above equation with the definition of the alpha vacua (47) and the definition of the in/out vacua (64), we can immediately see that

$$ \displaystyle\ket{{\rm out},+}=\ket*{\alpha^{\rm out}_+}, \displaystyle\ket{{\rm in},+}=\ket*{\alpha^{\rm in}_+}, \displaystyle\ket{{\rm out},-}=\ket*{\alpha^{\rm out}_-}, \displaystyle\ket{{\rm in},-}=\ket*{\alpha^{\rm in}_-}, $$

where we define $\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}$ by

$$ \displaystyle\tanh\alpha^{\rm out}_{+} \displaystyle=e^{+\pi ih_{+}}, \displaystyle\tanh\alpha^{\rm out}_{-} \displaystyle=e^{+\pi ih_{-}}, \displaystyle\tanh\alpha^{\rm in}_{+} \displaystyle=e^{-\pi ih_{+}}, \displaystyle\tanh\alpha^{\rm in}_{-} \displaystyle=e^{-\pi ih_{-}}. $$

We have now shown that the in/out vacua are $\alpha$ -vacua and have solved for the corresponding $\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}$ ’s for all $d$ and $m$ . The properties of the in/out vacua change qualitatively depending on whether $d$ is even or odd and whether the mass $m$ is heavy or light. Let us now go over all four cases separately. For heavy scalars we’ll define

$$ h_{\pm}=\frac{d-1}{2}\pm i\mu,\hskip 28.45274pt\mu=\sqrt{m^{2}-\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right)^{2}}>0, $$

and for light scalars we’ll define

$$ h_{\pm}=\frac{d-1}{2}\pm\nu,\hskip 28.45274pt\nu=\sqrt{\left(\frac{d-1}{2}\right)^{2}-m^{2}}>0. $$

#### Heavy scalar, $d$ odd:

The solutions to (71) in this case are

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm out}_{+} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{e^{ \pi\mu}+1}{e^{ \pi\mu} - 1}), \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm out}_{-} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{e^{\pi\mu} + 1}{e^{\pi\mu} - 1})+\frac{i\pi}{2}, \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm in}_{+} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{e^{\pi\mu} + 1}{e^{\pi\mu} - 1})+\frac{i\pi}{2}, \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm in}_{-} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{e^{ \pi\mu}+1}{e^{ \pi\mu} - 1}). $$

Notice that

$$ \real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out}_{+}})=\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm in}_{-}})>0,\hskip 28.45274pt\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out}_{-}})=\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm in}_{+}})<0, $$

so only $\ket{{\rm out},+}$ and $\ket{{\rm in},-}$ are normalizable. $\ket{{\rm out},-}$ and $\ket{{\rm in},+}$ are not normalizable. Furthermore, because $e^{\pi ih_{+}}=e^{-\pi ih_{-}}$ in odd dimensions,

$$ \alpha^{\rm out}_{+}=\alpha^{\rm in}_{-} $$

which implies

$$ \ket{{\rm in},-}=\ket{{\rm out},+}. $$

We have now given a simple proof of the famous fact that the “in” vacuum equals the “out” vacuum for a heavy field in odd spacetime dimension. This fact was originally discovered by Bousso, Maloney, and Strominger in Bousso et al. (2002). Later, in a beautiful work by Lagogiannis, Maloney, and Wang Lagogiannis et al. (2011), it was shown that the wave equation in odd dimensional de Sitter space can be recast into a problem in 1D supersymmetric quantum mechanics, and in that setting this fact can also be easily derived.

#### Heavy scalar, $d$ even:

The solutions to (71) here are

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm out}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{1 - i e^{ \mp\pi\mu}}{1 + i e^{ \mp\pi\mu} }), \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm in}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{1 + i e^{ \pm\pi\mu}}{1 -
i e^{ \pm\pi\mu} }). $$

Note that $\alpha^{\rm in/out}_{\pm}\in i\mathbb{R}$ . Furthermore,

$$ \real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out}_{+}})=\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm in}_{-}})>0\hskip 28.45274pt\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out}_{-}})=\real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm in}_{+}})<0 $$

so again only $\ket{{\rm out},+}$ and $\ket{{\rm in},-}$ are normalizable. However now

$$ \alpha^{\rm out}_{+}=(\alpha^{\rm in}_{-})^{*} $$

and therefore $\ket{{\rm out},+}$ and $\ket{{\rm in},-}$ are not the same state like they were in odd dimensions.

#### Light scalar, $d$ odd:

Light scalars are fundamentally different from heavy scalars. The solutions to (71) become

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm out}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\cot\frac{\pi\nu}{2} )\pm(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{i\pi}{4}\,, \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm in}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log( \cot\frac{\pi\nu}{2} )\mp(-1)^{\frac{d-1}{2}}\frac{i\pi}{4}\,. $$

These equations imply

$$ \real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}})=0 $$

so strictly speaking, none of the states $\ket{{\rm out/in},\pm}$ are normalizable, but all of them are right at the edge of the normalizability condition (57). Notice that

$$ \alpha^{\rm out}_{\pm}=\alpha^{\rm in}_{\mp} $$

which implies

$$ \displaystyle\ket{{\rm in},+} \displaystyle=\ket{{\rm out},-}, \displaystyle\ket{{\rm in},-} \displaystyle=\ket{{\rm out},+}, $$

for light scalars in odd dimensions. One consequence of the above equation is that a classical field in de Sitter which goes as $e^{h_{\pm}t}$ in the far past evolves into a field which goes as $e^{-h_{\mp}t}$ in the far future, meaning the field “flips” the rate at which it decays at the two boundaries from $h_{\pm}$ to $h_{\mp}$ .

There is however a pathological case we will briefly mention. If $\nu\in\mathbb{Z}$ then $e^{\pi ih_{+}}=e^{\pi ih_{-}}$ , meaning the $e^{-h_{+}t}$ and $e^{-h_{-}t}$ modes at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ and the $e^{h_{+}t}$ and $e^{h_{-}t}$ modes at ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ cannot be separated out from the euclidean mode using the $t\mapsto t+i\pi$ shift as we did in (66). This implies that when $\nu\in\mathbb{Z}$ , the in/out vacua are not actually $\alpha$ -vacua and the entire analysis we’ve given breaks down.

#### Light scalar, $d$ even:

The solutions to (71) are

$$ \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm out}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{1 - i e^{\pm\pi i \nu}}{1 + i e^{\pm\pi i \nu}}), \displaystyle\alpha^{\rm in}_{\pm} \displaystyle=(-1)^{\frac{d}{2}}\frac{1}{2}\log(\frac{1 + i e^{\mp\pi i \nu}}{1 - i e^{\mp\pi i \nu}}). $$

Once again,

$$ \real(e^{2\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}})=0 $$

so all of the in/out vacua are on the edge of normalizability. Furthermore,

$$ \alpha^{\rm out}_{\pm}=(\alpha^{\rm in}_{\mp})^{*} $$

so generically we don’t have an equality between in/out vacua like we had in odd dimensions. However, for special values of the mass where $\nu\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2}$ , we have $e^{\pi ih_{-}}=e^{-\pi ih_{-}}$ and $e^{\pi ih_{+}}=e^{-\pi ih_{+}}$ , implying

$$ \ket{{\rm out},+}=\ket{{\rm in},+},\hskip 28.45274pt\ket{{\rm out},-}=\ket{{\rm in},-}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ if }\nu\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2}. $$

For these values of $\nu$ , a free field which at $t=-\infty$ comes in as $e^{h_{\pm}t}$ leaves at $t=+\infty$ as $e^{-h_{\pm}t}$ , meaning there is no “flipping” like we saw with light fields in odd dimensions.

There are $d-1$ possible half-integer values for $\nu$ , which are

$$ \nu\in\left\{\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\ldots,\frac{d-1}{2}\right\}. $$

The conformally coupled scalar $m^{2}=d(d-2)/4$ corresponds to $\nu=1/2$ . We note that the $\nu=(d-1)/2$ case, corresponding to a massless field $m=0$ , requires a bit more care in its analysis due to the zero mode. We are not providing that more careful analysis here. We also point out that the in/out vacua in the special case of the $d=4$ conformally coupled scalar were studied in the work Ng and Strominger (2013).

Finally, just like when $d$ is odd, for the pathological $\nu\in\mathbb{Z}$ case the in/out vacua are not actually $\alpha$ -vacua.

## 9 Wavefunctionals of $\alpha$ -vacua at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ (for odd $d$ and $m>\tfrac{d-1}{2}$ )

In this section we will study the $\alpha$ -vacua wavefunctionals at timelike infinity ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ using the path integral. We will restrict our attention to odd spacetime dimension $d$ and heavy mass $m>(d-1)/2$ . While we could do the $d$ even or light mass case if we wished, we are mainly interested in studying the basic features of this wavefunctional and therefore adopt these simplifications.

In subsection 9.1 we solve for the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ . In subsection 9.2 we solve for the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ . In subsection 9.3 we show how, for $|\alpha|\ll 1$ , the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ can also be prepared by moving the antipodal charge from $E$ to ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ / ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ in the path integral. In subsection 9.4 we explain why operator ordering problems prevent us from giving a similar analysis for the case of finite $\alpha$ .

We define ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ and ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ as the constant $t$ surfaces

$$ {\mathcal{I}^{+}}=\{(t=T,\Omega)\text{ surface}\},\hskip 14.22636pt{\mathcal{I}^{-}}=\{(t=-T,\Omega)\text{ surface}\},\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }T\to\infty. $$

### 9.1 Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$

The Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ , which we will denote as $\Psi_{0}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}[\varphi]$ , can be prepared by a path integral over the euclidean half-sphere followed by a lorentzian path integral from the equator $E$ to ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ .

$$ \varphi \Psi_{0}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}[\varphi]= $$

If one has a euclidean mode solution $f_{e}$ , then the annihilation operator $\hat{a}(f_{e})$ will annihilate the Bunch-Davies vacuum at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ because ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ is contractible using the euclidean section.

$$ \varphi a_{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}(f_{e}) \varphi = =0 $$

We will now use this fact to solve for the wavefunctional. It is a gaussian functional

$$ \Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B^{\mIp}_{0,\ell} c_{\ell m}^2 ) $$

for some normalization constant $\mathcal{N}^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}$ and coefficients $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ . We are only interested in solving for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ .

Consider a euclidean mode solution of the form

$$ f_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)=y_{e,\ell}(t)Y_{\ell m}(\Omega). $$

The equation

$$ \left(\hat{a}(f_{e,\ell m})\Psi_{0}^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}\right)[\varphi]=0 $$

becomes

$$ \Big(\frac{y_{e,\ell}(T)}{i\cosh^{d-1}T}\partialderivative{c_{\ell m}}-\dot{y}_{e,\ell}(T)c_{\ell m}\Big)\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B^{\mIp}_{0,\ell} c_{\ell m}^2 )=0 $$

which implies, as $T$ becomes large,

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}=\frac{e^{(d-1)T}}{i2^{d}}\frac{\dot{y}_{e,\ell}(T)}{y_{e,\ell}(T)}. $$

We therefore need to solve for the large $T$ behavior of $y_{e,\ell}$ in order to solve for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ .

This can be done using the following trick: earlier, we noted that a certain linear combination of euclidean and antipodally flipped euclidean modes sum together to produce an “out” mode. See equation (69). Therefore, if we know how the “out” mode behaves at $t=T$ and $t=-T$ , we can solve for the behavior of the euclidean modes at $t=T$ .

We will consider an “out $-$ ” mode which we’ll decompose as

$$ f_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega)=y_{o,\ell}(t)Y_{\ell m}(\Omega). $$

As we discussed earlier,66 6 see for instance (76) solutions to the Klein-Gordon equation which behave like $e^{-h_{-}t}$ at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ will behave like $e^{h_{+}t}$ at ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ when $d$ is odd. However, there is also a relative phase that the solution will obtain between ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ and ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ . This phase was solved for in Bousso et al. (2002); Lagogiannis et al. (2011).

Near ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ and ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ , this “out $-$ ” mode behaves like

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{o,\ell}(t) \displaystyle=e^{+i\theta_{\ell}}e^{-h_{-}t} \displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}y_{o,\ell}(t) \displaystyle=e^{-i\theta_{\ell}}e^{+h_{+}t} $$

and the phase $\theta_{\ell}$ is

$$ e^{2i\theta_{\ell}}=\prod_{n=1}^{\ell+(d-3)/2}\frac{\mu+in}{\mu-in}. $$

We now apply (69) and write

$$ f_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)-e^{\pi ih_{+}}f^{A}_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\propto f_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega). $$

This can be re-expressed as the matrix equation

$$ \begin{pmatrix}1&-e^{\pi ih_{+}}\\
-e^{\pi ih_{+}}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\\
f_{e,\ell m}^{A}(t,\Omega)\end{pmatrix}\propto\begin{pmatrix}f_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\\
f^{A}_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\end{pmatrix}. $$

Note that we have not yet fixed the overall proportionality constant for the function $f_{e,\ell m}$ . We now invert (102) and arbitrarily fix this constant with

$$ \begin{pmatrix}f_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\\
f^{A}_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&e^{\pi ih_{+}}\\
e^{\pi ih_{+}}&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}f_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\\
f^{A}_{o,\ell m}(t,\Omega)\end{pmatrix}. $$

Using the fact that $Y_{\ell m}(\Omega^{A})=(-1)^{\ell}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega)$ , the above equation implies the euclidean mode behaves at large times as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{e,\ell}(t) \displaystyle=e^{i\theta_{\ell}-h_{-}t}+(-1)^{\ell}e^{\pi ih_{+}}e^{-i\theta_{\ell}-h_{+}t}, \displaystyle\lim_{t\to-\infty}y_{e,\ell}(t) \displaystyle=e^{-i\theta_{\ell}+h_{+}t}+(-1)^{\ell}e^{\pi ih_{+}}e^{i\theta_{\ell}+h_{-}t}. $$

Plugging this into (97) we arrive at

$$ \displaystyle B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell} \displaystyle=\frac{ie^{(d-1)T}}{2^{d}}\frac{h_{-}e^{i\theta_{\ell}-h_{-}T}+h_{+}(-1)^{\ell}e^{\pi ih_{+}}e^{-i\theta_{\ell}-h_{+}T}}{e^{i\theta_{\ell}-h_{-}T}+(-1)^{\ell}e^{\pi ih_{+}}e^{-i\theta_{\ell}-h_{+}T}} \displaystyle=\frac{ie^{(d-1)T}}{2^{d}}\left(\frac{d-1}{2}+(-1)^{\ell}\mu\tan^{(-1)^{\ell}}(\theta_{\ell}+\mu T-\pi h_{+}/2)\right). $$

Now that we have solved for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ , we have solved for $\Psi^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0}[\varphi]$ . Notice that $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ contains an overall factor of $e^{(d-1)T}$ , which grows as $T\to\infty$ . This is the well-known infrared divergence of the de Sitter wavefunctional.

### 9.2 $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$

We write the wavefunctional of the $\alpha$ -vacuum at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ as

$$ \Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{\alpha}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{\alpha}\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B^{\mIp}_{\alpha,\ell} c_{\ell m}^2 ). $$

If one defines the $\alpha$ -rotated euclidean mode

$$ f_{\alpha,\ell m}(t,\Omega)=y_{\alpha,\ell}(t)Y_{\ell m}(\Omega) $$

by

$$ f_{\alpha,\ell m}(t,\Omega)=\cosh(\alpha)f_{e,\ell m}(t,\Omega)-\sinh(\alpha)f_{e,\ell m}^{A}(t,\Omega) $$

then one has

$$ y_{\alpha,\ell}(t)=\cosh( \alpha)\,y_{e,\ell}(t)-\sinh(\alpha)\,(-1)^{\ell}y_{e,\ell}(-t). $$

The equation

$$ \left(\hat{a}(f_{\alpha,\ell m})\Psi^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha}\right)[\varphi]=0 $$

becomes

$$ \Big(\frac{y_{\alpha,\ell}(T)}{i\cosh^{d-1}T}\partialderivative{c_{\ell m}}-\dot{y}_{\alpha,\ell}(T)c_{\ell m}\Big)\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B^{\mIp}_{\alpha,\ell} c_{\ell m}^2 )=0, $$

which then implies

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha,\ell}=\frac{e^{(d-1)T}}{i2^{d}}\frac{\dot{y}_{\alpha,\ell}(T)}{y_{\alpha,\ell}(T)}. $$

Because $y_{\alpha,\ell}(T)$ can be expressed given quantities we have already solved for earlier, we have now solved for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha,\ell}$ . The full expression with all quantities plugged in is not particularly enlightening.

The expression simplifies in the case of the “out $+$ ” vacuum to

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\ell}=\frac{e^{(d-1)T}}{i2^{d}}\frac{\dot{y}_{o,\ell}(T)}{y_{o,\ell}(T)}=\frac{i}{2^{d}}e^{(d-1)T}h_{-}. $$

Note that $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\ell}$ is $\ell$ -independent. The “out $+$ ” wavefunctional is

$$ \Psi_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+}}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+}}\exp( - \frac{i}{2^d} e^{(d-1)T} h_- \int d^{d-1}\Omega\, \varphi(\Omega)^2 ). $$

We can see that there is no entanglement in this state between any two points on ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ .

### 9.3 Path integral calculation of $\Psi^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha}[\varphi]$ for $|\alpha|\ll 1$

$$ m\to\infty\;\;\text{implies}\;\;\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\alpha^{\rm in}_{-}\to 0. $$

The non-local charge insertion will now have the effect of changing the boundary conditions of the lorentzian path integral from $\varphi$ at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and $\varphi^{\prime}$ at $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ to $\varphi+\frac{\alpha}{2}{\varphi^{\prime}}^{A}$ at $\mathcal{I}^{+}$ and $\varphi^{\prime}-\frac{\alpha}{2}\varphi^{A}$ at $\mathcal{I}^{-}$ .

Using the fact that

$$ \Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{-}}_{0}[\varphi]=(\Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}[\varphi])^{*} $$

(which follows from the fact that $\Psi^{E}_{0}[\varphi]$ is a purely real wavefunctional) we end up with the expression, for small $\alpha$ ,

$$ \Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{\alpha}[\varphi]=\int\mathcal{D}\varphi^{\prime}\mathcal{S}[\varphi+\tfrac{\alpha}{2}{\varphi^{\prime}}^{A},\varphi^{\prime}-\tfrac{\alpha}{2}\varphi^{A}](\Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}[\varphi^{\prime}])^{*}. $$

This expression, which we derived using the path integral, tells us how we can use $\Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{0}[\varphi]$ to solve for $\Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{+}}_{\alpha}[\varphi]$ .

Let us now compute the S-matrix. We decompose the inputs of $\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]$ as

$$ \varphi(\Omega)=\sum_{\ell,m}c_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega),\hskip 28.45274pt\varphi^{\prime}(\Omega)=\sum_{\ell,m}c^{\prime}_{\ell m}Y_{\ell m}(\Omega). $$

Because we are dealing with a free field theory, the S-matrix must be a gaussian of the form

$$ \mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]=\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{S}}\exp( i \sum_{\ell,m} (a_{\ell} (c_{\ell m})^2 +b_{\ell}( c_{\ell m} c'_{\ell m} ) + a_{\ell} (c'_{\ell m})^2 )) $$

for some real coefficients $a_{\ell}$ and $b_{\ell}$ and normalization constant $\mathcal{N}_{\mathcal{S}}$ .

In order to solve for $a_{\ell}$ and $b_{\ell}$ , we will use the following trick. Take any $f$ which solves $(\nabla^{2}-m^{2})f=0$ and consider inserting $a_{\Sigma}(f)$ , defined on some surface $\Sigma$ , into the lorentzian S-matrix path integral. $\Sigma$ can be freely deformed freely without affecting the path integral, so we can start by setting $\Sigma={\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ and then deform it to ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ , as in figure 14. This equality creates a differential equation which can be used to solve for $\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]$ .

For our choice of $f$ , we will use the “out $-$ ” function $f_{o,\ell m}$ from (98). Our surface-deformation trick then gives

*Figure 14: An insertion of $a_{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}(f)$ into the lorentzian path integral can be continuously deformed to $a_{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}(f)$ . This creates a differential equation which can then be used to solve for $\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]$ .*

$$ \displaystyle(\frac{y_{o,\ell}(T)}{i\cosh^{d-1}(T)} \displaystyle\partialderivative{c_{\ell m}}-\dot{y}_{o,\ell}(T)c_{\ell m})\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}] \displaystyle=(-\frac{y_{o,\ell}(-T)}{i\cosh^{d-1}(-T)}\partialderivative{c'_{\ell m}}-\dot{y}_{o,\ell}(-T)c^{\prime}_{\ell m})\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]. $$

Because $\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]$ is the product of an independent gaussian for each $\ell$ , $m$ , the above differential equation can be reduced to the 1-dimensional equation

$$ \displaystyle(\eta_{\ell}\partialderivative{c_{\ell m}}+\xi_{\ell}c_{\ell m})\exp(i (a_\ell c_{\ell m}^2 + b_\ell c_{\ell m} c_{\ell m}' + a_\ell{c'_{\ell m}}^2)) \displaystyle=(\eta_{\ell}^{*}\partialderivative{c'_{\ell m}}-\xi_{\ell}^{*}c^{\prime}_{\ell m})\exp(i (a_\ell c_{\ell m}^2 + b_\ell c_{\ell m} c_{\ell m}' + a_\ell{c'_{\ell m}}^2)) $$

for

$$ \eta_{\ell}=\frac{y_{o,\ell}(T)}{i\cosh^{d-1}(T)}=\frac{e^{i\theta_{\ell}-h_{-}T}}{i\cosh^{d-1}(T)},\hskip 28.45274pt\xi_{\ell}=-\dot{y}_{o,\ell}(T)=h_{-}e^{i\theta_{\ell}-h_{-}T}. $$

Equation (127) reduces to

$$ \displaystyle 2i\eta_{\ell}a_{\ell}+\xi_{\ell}=i\eta^{*}_{\ell}b_{\ell},\hskip 28.45274pti\eta_{\ell}b_{\ell}=2i\eta^{*}_{\ell}a_{\ell}-\xi^{*}_{\ell}, $$

which has solutions

$$ \displaystyle a_{\ell}=\frac{i}{2}\frac{\eta_{\ell}\xi_{\ell}+\eta_{\ell}^{*}\xi_{\ell}^{*}}{\eta_{\ell}^{2}-(\eta_{\ell}^{*})^{2}},\hskip 14.22636ptb_{\ell}=i\frac{\eta_{\ell}^{*}\xi_{\ell}+\eta_{\ell}\xi_{\ell}^{*}}{\eta_{\ell}^{2}-(\eta_{\ell}^{*})^{2}}. $$

The $a_{\ell}$ , $b_{\ell}$ coefficients then turn out to be, in the large $T$ limit,

$$ \displaystyle a_{\ell} \displaystyle=-\frac{e^{(d-1)T}}{2^{d}}\left(\frac{d-1}{2}-\mu\cot(2 (\theta_\ell+\mu T))\right), \displaystyle b_{\ell} \displaystyle=-\mu\frac{e^{(d-1)T}}{2^{d-1}}\csc(2 (\theta_\ell+\mu T)). $$

We have now computed the S-matrix, aside from the normalization constant which we will ignore.

With the free S-matrix, gaussian initial states will evolve into gaussian final states in the following way. For initial and final states

$$ \Psi_{\rm initial}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}[\varphi]\propto\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B_{{\rm initial}, \ell}^{\mIm} c_{\ell m}^2 ),\hskip 14.22636pt\Psi_{\rm final}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}[\varphi]\propto\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B_{{\rm final}, \ell}^{\mIp} c_{\ell m}^2 ), $$

related by

$$ \Psi_{\rm final}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}[\varphi]=\int\mathcal{D}\varphi^{\prime}\mathcal{S}[\varphi,\varphi^{\prime}]\,\Psi_{\rm initial}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}[\varphi^{\prime}], $$

the 1D gaussian integral

$$ \displaystyle\int dc_{\ell m}^{\prime} \displaystyle\exp( i (a_\ell c_{\ell m}^2 + b_\ell c_{\ell m} c_{\ell m}' + a_{\ell} {c_{\ell m}'}^2 ) )\exp( - B_{{\rm initial}, \ell}^{\mIm} c_{\ell m}'^2 ) \displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{B_{{\rm initial},\ell}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}-ia_{\ell}}}\exp(i (a_\ell- \frac{b_\ell^2}{4 a_\ell+ 4 i B_{{\rm initial}, \ell}^{\mIm}}) c_{\ell m}^2 ) $$

implies that the “ $B$ -coefficients” evolve from ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ to ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ as

$$ B_{{\rm initial},\ell}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}\longrightarrow B_{{\rm final},\ell}^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}=-i\left(a_{\ell}-\frac{b_{\ell}^{2}}{4a_{\ell}+4iB_{{\rm initial},\ell}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}}\right). $$

Let us now perform two checks on our S-matrix calculation. For our first check, let us confirm that the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ really does evolve into the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ .

If we write the Bunch-Davies wavefunctional on ${\mathcal{I}^{-}}$ as

$$ \Psi^{\mathcal{I}^{-}}_{0}[\varphi]=\mathcal{N}^{\mathcal{I}^{-}}_{0}\exp( - \sum_{\ell,m} B^{\mIm}_{0,\ell} c_{\ell m}^2 ). $$

then from (122) we know

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{0,\ell}=(B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell})^{*}. $$

Plugging in our known expressions for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{0,\ell}$ and $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}$ from (105) into (135), we do find that

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{0,\ell}\longrightarrow B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{0,\ell}\;\;\;\;\checkmark $$

as expected.

For our second check, let us confirm that the “in” vacuum really does evolve into the “out” vacuum, as we know it must in odd dimensions.

Because $\alpha^{\rm out/in}_{\pm}\in\mathbb{R}$ in odd dimensions, we know that

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{\alpha^{\rm in}_{-},\ell}=(B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\ell})^{*} $$

and thus, using our already known expressions for $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{\alpha^{\rm in}_{-},\ell}$ and $B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\ell}$ from (113), we can plug them into (135) and confirm that indeed

$$ B^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}_{\alpha^{\rm in}_{-},\ell}\longrightarrow B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha^{\rm out}_{+},\ell}\;\;\;\;\checkmark $$

as expected.

With our checks complete, let us now confirm that our path integral expression for the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional (123) really does hold when $\alpha$ is small.

Defining

$$ \displaystyle c^{\alpha}_{\ell m} \displaystyle\equiv c_{\ell m}+(-1)^{\ell}\frac{\alpha}{2}\,c^{\prime}_{\ell m} \displaystyle{c^{\alpha}_{\ell m}}^{\prime} \displaystyle\equiv c^{\prime}_{\ell m}-(-1)^{\ell}\frac{\alpha}{2}\,c_{\ell m} $$

one can compute the 1D integral

$$ \displaystyle\int dc_{\ell m}^{\prime} \displaystyle\exp( i (a_\ell(c^\alpha_{\ell m})^2 + b_\ell(c^\alpha_{\ell m} {c^\alpha_{\ell m}}') + a_{\ell} ({c_{\ell m}^\alpha}')^2 ) )\exp( - B^{\mIm}_{0,\ell} c_{\ell m}'^2 ) \displaystyle\propto\exp( - \left( - i a_\ell+ i (-1)^\ell\frac{\alpha}{2} b_\ell+ \frac{b^2}{4 B^{\mIm}_{0,\ell} - 4 i a_\ell- 2 i (-1)^\ell\alpha b_\ell} \right) c_{\ell m}^2 ) $$

to the first order in $\alpha$ (where we have dropped the $c_{\ell m}$ -independent normalization constant out front). This 1D integral computes the $\alpha$ -vacuum wavefunctional at ${\mathcal{I}^{+}}$ . Comparing the $B$ -coefficients, we find that indeed

$$ -ia_{\ell}+i(-1)^{\ell}\frac{\alpha}{2}b_{\ell}+\frac{b^{2}}{4B_{0,\ell}^{{\mathcal{I}^{-}}}-4ia_{\ell}-2i(-1)^{\ell}\alpha b_{\ell}}=B^{{\mathcal{I}^{+}}}_{\alpha,\ell}+\mathcal{O}(\alpha^{2})\;\;\;\;\checkmark $$

which confirms that (123) computes the $\alpha$ -vacuum out state for small $\alpha$ .
